title: Methodology
text:
This project examines the World Bank Group’s financing relationship with Costa Rica from 1980 to 2025. The central question is how that relationship evolved across four decades — in scale, instruments, sectoral priorities, and stated development objectives — and what the evolution reveals about the intersection of Costa Rica’s development trajectory and the World Bank Group’s changing institutional practice.
The analysis is explicitly not a causal study. It does not test whether World Bank lending caused changes in GDP, inequality, health, or other outcomes. It examines the portfolio itself and the context in which it operated.
Unit of analysis: Individual projects and loans, aggregated by year, period, and sector.
Geographic scope: Costa Rica only. Findings are not representative of the World Bank Group’s global portfolio or of developing-country experience generally.
Study period: 1980–2025 inclusive. Pre-1980 records are retained for reference but excluded from primary totals and charts. Three projects approved in 2025 are included. Records from 2026 are outside scope.

3. Project universe reconciliation
The Projects & Operations List contains 115 Costa Rica project records. The IBRD Statement contains 68 loan records for 59 unique project IDs. The WB Projects API V2 extract contains 72 project records.

The 43 projects in the Projects List but not in the API fall into four categories: 1. Legacy P006xxx-numbered projects not indexed in the V2 API search system (pre-2000). 2. Grants, GEF trust-fund operations, and other non-IBRD financing types. 3. Early-1990s IBRD loans not returned by the API. 4. P148435 ($420M, 2016) — the most significant missing project.
For IBRD financial analysis, only the 59 project IDs with loan records are used. Projects Board Approved but without loan records, and grants or trust funds, are excluded from financial totals.

text:
4. Treatment of project approval dates
The V2 API extract had missing boardapprovaldate for 16 projects. A three-stage date recovery process was conducted:








Stage
Method
Outcome




Phase 0
V2 API extract
16 projects with NULL boardapprovaldate


Phase 1
V3 API + WB bulk Excel (downloaded 2026-10-30)
15/16 dates recovered; V3 and Excel agreed on all 15


Final

The one permanently unresolved project is P169724 (Learning for All, Dropped, $100 million planned). There is no approval date in any source for this project; it was likely never board-approved.
All recovered and original dates are compared against the Projects & Operations List. Where dates differ between sources, the Projects List is used as authoritative.

title: Methodology
text:
5. IBRD financial definitions
All IBRD amounts are from the IBRD Statement of Loans and Guarantees, snapshot 09/30/2026.







Term
Definition




Original Principal Amount
Loan amount as approved by the IBRD Board, in nominal US dollars at time of approval


Cancelled Amount
Portions of the principal cancelled — unused balances at close, mid-project reductions, or full cancellation of Terminated loans


Net Principal
original_principal - cancelled_amount. Represents the commitment net of cancellations. Not “money received.”


Undisbursed Amount
Remaining balance not drawn, converted at end-period exchange rate


Disbursed Amount
Cumulative drawdowns since inception. Not an annual flow. Cannot be assigned to approval year.


Repaid to IBRD
Cumulative principal repaid


Due to IBRD
Outstanding principal




Primary analytical measure
Original Principal Amount is used as the primary measure of approved lending scale. It maps cleanly to the approval year, is unambiguous (it was set at the board meeting), and allows comparison across time. Net principal is reported alongside it but not used as the primary measure for trend charts.
Real amounts use the formula: real_2025 = nominal * (defl_2025 / defl_approval_year), where defl_x is the World Bank GDP deflator value (NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS) for year x.


Cumulative disbursements and annual flows
The disbursed amounts in the IBRD Statement are cumulative balances as of 09/30/2026. They cannot be assigned to the approval year and do not represent annual disbursement flows. Annual disbursement data would require transaction-level records from the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics (IDS) or equivalent sources, which are not part of the current dataset.


Cancellations
Three loans have “Terminated” status: P006945, P006942, P006940. For these, original principal equals cancelled amount (net = 0); they were approved but the loan agreements were never signed or the loans never became effective. They are included in project counts but excluded from net principal totals.

6. Instrument classification
IBRD loan types in the Statement (CPL, FSL, NPL, SCL, SCPD) are financial-term codes, not operational instrument types. Classification as Development Policy Loan or Investment Project Financing uses the following logic, applied in 04_prepare_ibrd.R:







Classified as DPL
Reason

P111926 (CAT DDO, 2008)
Contingent credit line (DDO = deferred drawdown, policy-based)

“Public Finance and Competitiveness Development Policy Loan”

“Second Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Loan”


P181372 (2024)
“Social Risk Management DPL DDO”


P508347 (2025)
“Fiscal Management and Green Growth” — confirmed DPL in project description



All other projects are classified as Investment Project Financing.
Manual override table: data/manual/instrument_overrides.csv
A small number of projects require manual overrides that cannot be reliably captured by automated name or loan-type rules. Manual overrides are stored separately from the automated rules, so the automated result remains visible for auditing. The final classification (instrument_group) uses the override where one exists; instrument_group_auto preserves the automated result.
Current overrides:









Project

Reason




P006919 (Highway, 1980)
DPL (NPL rule)

Road rehabilitation and equipment financing; NPL loan type alone does not establish policy-based character. Manual check confirmed investment lending.


P006922 (Export Dev., 1983)

SAL-era companion adjustment operation. Classified as DPL on analytical grounds: the operation supported export-sector liberalisation as part of the structural adjustment programme.



The instrument classification review table is saved to data/derived/instrument_classification_review.csv and includes every in-scope project, its loan type codes, automated basis, final classification, and any override reason. The NPL loan type is flagged in that review as requiring individual examination, since P006919 demonstrates that NPL alone is not sufficient to establish DPL status.
Note: Several 1980s-era projects (P006933 Technical Assistance, P006924 Atlantic Agriculture, P006926 Transport Sector, P006938 Basic Education, P006941 Water Supply, P006954 Health Sector) had supplemental SCPD companion loans — a “policy tranche” common in the SAL era — but are classified as Investment Project Financing because the primary CPL loan funded investment activity. Only the pure SAL/structural adjustment operations are classified as DPL.

title: Methodology
text:
7. Sector classification
Sector information comes from two sources: 1. WB Projects API V2 (sector1, sector2, sector3 with name and percentage) 2. Projects & Operations List (Sector 1, 2, 3 — name only, no percentages)
API sector data is preferred; Projects List names supplement where API is unavailable.
Where sector percentages are available and approximately complete, project financing is allocated proportionally across sectors. For example, a $100M project with Sector 1 at 60% and Sector 2 at 40% contributes $60M and $40M respectively to sector totals. This avoids double-counting project principal.
Coverage: Sector data is available for 22 of 35 in-scope IBRD projects, representing approximately $2.7 billion of $4.6 billion in original principal (~59%). The 2020–2025 DPL series lacks sector percentage data, significantly understating recent operations in sector charts.
P178320 treatment: The API records sector allocations for P178320 (COVID-19 Vaccines, Terminated), but the IBRD statement records its original principal as $0. That project is excluded from dollar-allocation totals but retained in project counts where sector names appear.
Ten broad sector groups are defined in functions.R: group_sector().

title: Methodology
text:
8. Inflation adjustment
Primary index: US GDP deflator, indicator NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS, retrieved from World Bank API (api.worldbank.org/v2/country/US/indicator/NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS).
Base year: 2020 = 100 (as returned by the API).
Coverage: 1960–2025, no missing years.
Why GDP deflator (not CPI): CPI measures consumer price changes affecting US households; the GDP deflator measures price changes across all US-produced final goods and services. For comparing the real scale of historical dollar-denominated financial commitments, the GDP deflator is more appropriate.
Limitations: - Neither index measures the local purchasing power of lending in Costa Rica. - The 2025 deflator value is preliminary and may be revised in future WB data vintages. - A $100M loan in 1985 purchased different quantities of Costa Rican infrastructure than $100M in 2020.
Validation: The 1980→2025 multiplier is approximately 3.275 (~$328M in 2025 USD per $100M in 1980).

title: Methodology
text:
9. IFC methodology
IFC investment amounts represent IFC’s own-account investment in private entities and are fundamentally different from IBRD sovereign loan principal. They are never combined with IBRD figures.
Date caveat: Only 2 IFC projects (Advisory Services) have actual Approval Date values. All Investment projects show Projected Board Date — a planned date, not an actual approval confirmation. Year assignments from IFC data are approximate.
Amount parsing: The Investment as Approved by The Board field in the IFC Excel contains text such as “15.0 million (USD)…”. Investment amounts are extracted by parsing the leading number.
Deduplication: The source file contains 40 rows for 30 unique project numbers (10 projects have multiple disclosure documents). The final dataset uses one row per project number, taking the first non-missing value for each field.
Known issues documented in 05_prepare_ifc.R: BAC CR Green ($200M, 2025 — $30M unfunded guarantee line excluded from investment amount), Coopenae ($15M IFC of $30M total package), Aeropuerto Juan Santamaría ($35M), Corporacion Supermercados Unidos ($40M, multi-country scope), Insulet CR ($97M, pipeline/excluded).

title: Methodology
text:
10. MIGA methodology
MIGA Gross Exposure Up to represents the maximum possible MIGA liability under issued guarantee contracts, not a loan or capital transfer.
Fiscal year: MIGA uses World Bank fiscal years (July 1 – June 30). FY2008 = July 2007 – June 2008.
Deduplication: Project 3639 (Grupo del Istmo de Papagayo) appears three times in the source data (FY2001, FY2002, FY2003) with amounts of $16.4M, $38.3M, and $81M respectively. These represent successive disclosure events for the same development, not three independent guarantees. The FY2001 and FY2002 rows are removed; FY2003 ($81M) is used as the canonical record representing peak exposure. Summing all three rows would overstate by ~$136M.

title: Methodology
text:
11. IDA context
Costa Rica’s last IDA credit was in FY1962 (source: World Bank IDA Graduates page). The 1980–2025 analysis is entirely IBRD. The IBRD Statement contains no IDA transactions for Costa Rica.

title: Methodology
section: 12. Calendar year vs fiscal year conventions
text:
12. Calendar year vs fiscal year conventions
IBRD and the Projects & Operations List use calendar-year board approval dates. IFC and MIGA use World Bank fiscal years (July–June). This project uses calendar years for the primary IBRD analysis. IFC and MIGA dates are labelled as approximate or fiscal-year as appropriate.

title: Methodology
text:
14. Reproducibility
The complete analysis can be rebuilt from raw source files.
Prerequisites: R ≥ 4.4, Quarto ≥ 1.4, R packages listed in R/00_setup.R.
Pipeline (run in order from project root):
source("R/01_import_sources.R") # documentation only
source("R/02_prepare_wdi.R")    # deflator and WDI (requires internet)
source("R/03_reconcile_projects.R")
source("R/04_prepare_ibrd.R")
source("R/05_prepare_ifc.R")
source("R/06_prepare_miga.R")
source("R/07_analysis.R")
source("R/08_visualizations.R")
source("R/09_validation.R")     # all checks should pass
Then render the site:
quarto render
Scripts requiring internet access: 02_prepare_wdi.R (World Bank API calls for deflator and WDI indicators). All other scripts read only from data/raw/ or earlier pipeline outputs in data/processed/.
Raw files in data/raw/ must be preserved unchanged. The archive/ directory contains historical exploratory scripts from Phase 0 and Phase 1; they are not part of the active pipeline.

section: B. Nominal versus real: the inflation story
text:
B. Nominal versus real: the inflation story









In real 2025 dollars, the 1980s SAL era (4 policy-based projects, ~$235M nominal) represented approximately $772M — substantially larger than the nominal figure suggests. The 2009 $500M DPL was approximately $728M in 2025 dollars. The recent 2020–2025 operations lose some of their comparative magnitude once inflation-adjusted.
Real amounts use the US GDP deflator (NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS, base 2020=100). The 2025 deflator value is preliminary.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica occupies a narrow strip of land between Nicaragua and Panama — home to roughly five million people and an extraordinary diversity of wildlife. It abolished its army in 1948. By the early 2000s it had achieved life expectancy comparable to the United States and near-universal access to education and healthcare, all on an income level that placed it squarely in the middle of the global middle class.
It is also a country that has borrowed substantially from the World Bank for 45 years.
This project examines that borrowing — not as a simple story of a donor and a recipient, but as an evolving relationship between two institutions responding to shifting circumstances, changing ideas about development, and their own strategic priorities. The central question is:

How did the World Bank’s financing relationship with Costa Rica change from 1980 to 2025 — in its scale, its instruments, and its stated priorities — and what does it reveal about the changing practice of international development finance?

The analysis is descriptive. It documents patterns in a 45-year lending record and explores what those patterns might reflect. It does not establish that World Bank lending caused changes in Costa Rica’s economy or society.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica occupies a narrow strip of land between Nicaragua and Panama — home to roughly five million people and an extraordinary diversity of wildlife. It abolished its army in 1948. By the early 2000s it had achieved life expectancy comparable to the United States and near-universal access to education and healthcare, all on an income level that placed it squarely in the middle of the global middle class.
It is also a country that has borrowed substantially from the World Bank for 45 years.
This project examines that borrowing — not as a simple story of a donor and a recipient, but as an evolving relationship between two institutions responding to shifting circumstances, changing ideas about development, and their own strategic priorities. The central question is:

How did the World Bank’s financing relationship with Costa Rica change from 1980 to 2025 — in its scale, its instruments, and its stated priorities — and what does it reveal about the changing practice of international development finance?

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: Who does what: the World Bank Group
text:
Who does what: the World Bank Group
The term “World Bank” can be confusing because it refers to several related but distinct institutions. This project covers three of them.
IBRD — the core lender. The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development makes long-maturity loans to creditworthy middle-income governments. Costa Rica has been an IBRD borrower throughout the study period. This is the main subject of the analysis.
IFC — the private-sector arm. The International Finance Corporation invests in private companies — banks, manufacturers, energy producers, agribusinesses — not governments. It operates separately from the IBRD and reports different kinds of amounts. IFC investment in Costa Rica is substantial and concentrated in financial services and clean energy.
MIGA — the guarantee agency. The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency issues political-risk guarantees to private investors. MIGA does not lend money; it backs private investment decisions by absorbing certain political risks. Its Costa Rica portfolio spans tourism, infrastructure, and banking.

Important: These institutions’ numbers cannot be added together. An IBRD loan, an IFC equity investment, and a MIGA guarantee exposure are three different things — different instruments, different financial measures, different kinds of risk. This analysis presents them separately.

A note on IDA: a fourth institution, the International Development Association, provides concessional financing to the world’s poorest countries. Costa Rica’s last IDA credit was in FY1962. The 1980–2025 analysis is entirely IBRD.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Four decades of IBRD lending
Between 1980 and 2025, the IBRD approved 35 projects in Costa Rica with a combined original principal of $4.6B in nominal US dollars — roughly $6.2B in constant 2025 values.
Thirty-four of those projects involved financial commitments; the thirty-fifth (a COVID-19 vaccine operation approved in 2022) was terminated before the loan agreement was signed, so its original principal in the IBRD’s records is $0.





Annual IBRD commitments to Costa Rica, 1980–2025. Each bar shows original principal at board approval (the amount approved by the IBRD Board). Lighter bars show the same amounts adjusted to constant 2025 USD using the US GDP deflator. The 2022 near-zero bar reflects a vaccine operation that was board-approved but terminated before the loan agreement was signed.




The lending record divides into four broad periods, each shaped by distinct conditions.

The 1980s: debt crisis and structural adjustment
Costa Rica entered the 1980s in economic distress. Between 1979 and 1982, GDP contracted sharply, inflation approached 90%, and the country defaulted on its external debt — the result of commodity price shocks, rising US interest rates, and regional instability. The World Bank, working alongside the International Monetary Fund and USAID, responded with a series of Structural Adjustment Loans.
Structural adjustment remains controversial. The loans provided foreign currency to keep the government solvent; in exchange, Costa Rica agreed to reform its trade policy, reduce state involvement in markets, and restructure public enterprises. SAL I arrived in 1985, SAL II in 1988, and SAL III — extending into the following decade — in 1993.
The Bank also financed more conventional investment alongside adjustment: water supply, petroleum sector assistance, and road rehabilitation. In total, the 1980s saw eight IBRD projects worth $294M in nominal terms — roughly $772M in today’s dollars. Around 70% of that sum, by original principal, went to policy-based adjustment lending; the remainder financed identifiable infrastructure and investment activities.


The 1990s and 2000s: investment and diversification
After the adjustment era, the IBRD shifted toward identifiable projects: health system reform, education equity, payment for environmental services, environmental policy, and urban infrastructure. A “catastrophe deferred drawdown option” credit in 2008 provided a disaster-risk buffer that could be called on after a major natural disaster.
A distinctive thread through this period was environmental finance. In 2000, the Bank provided $33 million for the Ecomarkets project, supporting Costa Rica’s pioneering program of payments to landowners for maintaining forest cover. This form of conservation finance — paying for ecosystem services — was largely novel at the time. When the global financial crisis hit in 2008–2009, the Bank approved a $500 million Development Policy Loan for public finance and competitiveness, one of two $500 million operations in the entire portfolio.


The 2010s: two large investments
A decade that might appear lean on the charts was not. It held only two IBRD projects — but they were substantial.
The 2012 Higher Education Improvement loan ($200 million) supported Costa Rica’s public university system. The 2016 Strengthening Universal Health Insurance loan ($420 million) supported the Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social (CCSS), which administers Costa Rica’s universal health care system. The health insurance loan is the single largest investment-type operation in the entire 1980–2025 portfolio. It was conspicuously absent from an earlier version of this analysis due to a data gap in the World Bank’s project API — an omission that invalidated previous conclusions about the period.


The 2020s: fiscal reform, climate, and pandemic
The 2020–2025 period accounts for 57.9% of all nominal 1980–2025 commitments — twelve projects totalling $2.66 billion. Several forces converged: the COVID-19 crisis, Costa Rica’s long-building fiscal consolidation (anchored by a 2018 tax reform), and the country’s national Decarbonization Plan targeting net-zero emissions by 2050.
The Bank’s response included a series of large Development Policy Loans that linked fiscal reform directly to climate objectives — the Fiscal and Decarbonization DPL series. This pattern — budget support tied simultaneously to fiscal adjustment and green investment — reflects changes in both World Bank strategy and in how Costa Rica frames its own development priorities.





IBRD lending by instrument type. Development Policy Loans (DPLs) provide budget support tied to policy commitments; Investment Project Financing (IPF) funds identifiable programs and capital projects.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Where the money went (with caveats)
The chart below shows how lending was distributed across sectors — with an important limitation. The 2020–2025 DPL series, which accounts for more than half of that period’s lending by value, does not come with traditional sector percentages, because DPLs operate through government policy rather than specific investment activities. The chart therefore represents only the portion of the portfolio where sector allocations are recorded, covering about 59% of total original principal ($2.7 billion of $4.6 billion).





Sectoral composition of IBRD lending where sector data is available. The chart covers 22 of 35 in-scope projects, representing approximately $2.7 billion — roughly 59% of total original principal. The 2020–2025 DPL series is largely excluded because DPLs are not assigned traditional sector percentages.




Within this partial picture: transportation and infrastructure dominated the early portfolio; finance and public administration grew steadily; education and health were persistent investment targets; and environment, agriculture, and natural resources formed a consistent thread throughout.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: What the Bank said it was doing
text:
What the Bank said it was doing
The Bank publishes a project abstract for most operations — a statement of objectives and intended activities. The chart below tracks how often certain thematic areas appeared in those abstracts, by period.
This is an analysis of institutional language, not of outcomes or priorities. The 1990s are entirely absent because no abstracts are available for that decade in the data source used here.





Thematic keyword presence in project abstracts by period. The shaded 1990–1999 column has no available abstracts and is excluded. Percentages are shares of projects with available abstracts, not all in-scope projects. Themes are not mutually exclusive.




With those caveats, a pattern emerges: environmental and climate language appears in every period with available abstracts, but changes character. In the 2000s it appears in specific conservation projects; by the 2020s it is embedded in fiscal and macroeconomic operations. Governance and fiscal language surges in the 2020s, reflecting the DPL series. Infrastructure language is strong early and fades as direct infrastructure lending does.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica’s development trajectory





Costa Rica’s development trajectory. These are contextual patterns, not evidence of causation.




Costa Rica’s improvement on most standard development measures over this period has been substantial. GDP per capita — in current US dollars, unadjusted for inflation — grew from roughly $2,000 in 1980 to $18,900 in 2024. Life expectancy rose from 73 years to 81 years.
Inequality is more complicated. The Gini index reached its highest recorded level around 51.8 in 2002 before declining through the 2000s and 2010s. It rose modestly in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, then resumed declining to around 45.5 by 2025.
What none of this tells us is why these things happened. World Bank lending may have contributed to Costa Rica’s development record — or it may have been incidental to changes driven by Costa Rica’s own institutions, demographic trends, trade patterns, and policy choices. The correlation between lending episodes and development trends is worth noting; establishing causation from these data is not possible.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
IFC: private investment





IFC own-account investments in Costa Rica by sector and indicative board date (nominal USD). Dates are projected board dates, not confirmed approvals. IFC investment amounts are not comparable to IBRD sovereign lending.




Alongside IBRD lending, IFC has made 23 investments in Costa Rican businesses with indicative own-account amounts totalling approximately $874 million (nominal USD). The portfolio is dominated by financial services — commercial banks, SME lenders, housing finance institutions — consistent with IFC’s mandate in middle-income countries. The largest single non-financial investment is the $100 million Reventazon hydroelectric project (2012).
IFC invests in private entities on commercial terms. Its amounts cannot be compared with IBRD principal or summed to produce a “World Bank Group total.”

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
MIGA: de-risking private capital
Between 1995 and FY2008, MIGA issued guarantee contracts covering 10 Costa Rica projects (deduplicated). The portfolio spans tourism, banking, power generation, manufacturing, and transportation. MIGA’s financial measure — gross exposure — is the maximum potential liability under issued guarantees, not a loan or a disbursement. The largest guarantee ($158.5 million) covered an investment in the Autopistas del Sol toll road concession (FY2008).

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: What we can and cannot say
text:
What we can and cannot say
What the evidence supports:

IBRD engagement with Costa Rica has been continuous across four decades but has changed character substantially: from adjustment lending in the 1980s, to project investment in health, education, and environment, to large policy-based operations for fiscal reform and decarbonization in the 2020s.
Environmental and climate concerns appear in every lending period, but their character shifts — from ring-fenced conservation projects to goals embedded in fiscal policy.
Both 2009 and 2023 saw $500 million IBRD commitments, tied respectively to global financial crisis response and the Fiscal and Decarbonization DPL series.
IFC’s presence complements IBRD lending by working in the private sector; the two operate under different mandates and their financial measures are not interchangeable.

What the evidence cannot tell us:

Whether World Bank lending caused improvements in Costa Rica’s health, education, or environmental outcomes.
Whether structural adjustment conditions of the 1980s and 1990s helped or hurt Costa Rican workers and households.
Whether the Bank’s current climate-focused DPL structure is driving Costa Rica’s decarbonization ambitions or largely ratifying ambitions the country was already pursuing.
How this portfolio compares to comparable countries, or what it would look like if either party had made different choices.


Explore the evidence in the Analysis section, check the sources and methods in Methodology, and look up variable definitions in the Data Dictionary.

IBRD projects (data/processed/ibrd_projects.csv)
Unit: One row per project (aggregated from loan records). Join key: project_id.



IBRD projects — variable definitions (project-level aggregates)


Variable
Definition
Derivation




project_id
World Bank project ID
From ibrd_loans_clean


n_loans
Number of loan records for this project
count() over project_id


approval_year
Calendar year of first loan's board approval
first(approval_year)


board_date
Parsed board approval date
first(board_date)


period
Period grouping
first(period)


instrument_group
Final instrument type (after overrides)
paste(unique()); uses overrides from data/manual/


instrument_group_auto
Automated instrument type (before overrides)
paste(unique()); preserved for auditing


override_applied
Whether any manual override applies
any(override_applied)


override_reason
Reason for the manual override, if applied
first(na.omit(override_reason))


loan_type_codes
All loan type codes for this project
paste(unique(loan_type))


loan_status_summary
All loan statuses
paste(unique(loan_status))


total_principal
Sum of original_principal_amount_us across all loans
sum()


total_cancelled
Sum of cancelled_amount_us across all loans
sum()


total_disbursed
Sum of disbursed_amount_us (cumulative, snapshot balance)
sum()


total_repaid
Sum of repaid_to_ibrd_us
sum()


net_principal
pmax(total_principal - total_cancelled, 0)
Capped at 0; see loan-level notes for P178320


real_principal_2025
Sum of real_principal_2025 across loans
sum()


project_name
Project name (from Projects List if available, else loan)
Left join to projects_universe


sector1_xl, sector2_xl, sector3_xl
Sector classifications from Projects List
Left join to projects_universe


in_scope
Whether approval_year is in 1980–2025
Derived

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Projects universe (data/processed/projects_universe.csv)
Unit: One row per project from the Projects & Operations List. 115 total. Source hierarchy: Projects List is authoritative.



Projects universe — variable definitions


Variable
Definition
Notes




project_id
World Bank project ID
Primary key


project_name
Project name from Projects List



board_date_xl
Board approval date (parsed from Projects List)



approval_year
Calendar year of board approval
Derived from board_date_xl


period
Period grouping
1980–1989 … 2020–2025 + Pre-1980 + Post-scope


last_stage
Last Stage Reached in the project pipeline
Board Approved / CD Approved / Concept Review / etc.


financing_type
Financing type: IBRD / Grants / Other / NA
NA for legacy records without this field


is_ibrd_loan
financing_type == 'IBRD'
Logical


is_grant
financing_type == 'Grants'
Logical


has_loan_record
Whether this project_id has a record in the IBRD Statement
Logical; defines IBRD-eligible set


in_scope
Whether approval_year is in 1980–2025
Logical


ibrd_commit_xl
IBRD Commitment from Projects List
Character field; converted to numeric; NA for many rows


sector1_xl, sector2_xl, sector3_xl
Sector fields from Projects List



pdo
Project Development Objective
From Projects List

title: Data Dictionary
text:
IFC projects (data/processed/ifc_projects.csv)
Unit: One row per unique IFC project number (deduplicated from 40 disclosure rows to 30 projects).



IFC projects — variable definitions


Variable
Definition
Notes




project_number
IFC project number
Primary key


project_name
IFC project name



type_desc
Investment or Advisory Services



status
Active / Completed / Pending



sector
Full IFC sector classification code and name
Granular IFC taxonomy


sector_group
Simplified sector grouping
Derived: Financial Services / Energy / Tourism etc.


approval_date_act
Actual Approval Date
Available only for 2 Advisory Services projects


projected_board_dt
Projected Board Date
PLANNED date, not confirmed approval


best_date
Coalesce(approval_date_act, projected_board_dt)
Best available date proxy


best_year
Year from best_date
Use with caution; projected dates only for investments


date_type
Describes which date was used
'Actual (Advisory only)' or 'Projected board date (indicative)'


ifc_invest_usd_m
IFC own-account investment amount in USD millions
Parsed from 'Investment as Approved by The Board' text field


n_docs
Number of disclosure documents for this project



is_advisory
type_desc == 'Advisory Services'



is_investment
type_desc == 'Investment'



is_pipeline
status == 'Pending'
Insulet CR (51930) — excluded from historical analysis


in_scope
best_year >= 1980 & best_year <= 2025







IFC amounts are indicative and NOT comparable to IBRD sovereign loan principal. They represent IFC’s own-account investment in private entities. The investment_text field also includes syntax from the disclosure portal; amounts are extracted from the leading number.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
MIGA projects (data/processed/miga_projects.csv)
Unit: One row per deduplicated project (10 projects from 12 source rows; project 3639 uses FY2003 as canonical record).



MIGA projects — variable definitions


Variable
Definition
Notes




project_id
MIGA project identifier
Integer


title
Project title



sector
Sector (Tourism / Banking / Power / Transportation / Manufacturing)



fiscal_year
MIGA fiscal year of guarantee issuance
FY = July–June; FY2008 = July 2007–June 2008


fy_label
Integer copy of fiscal_year for filtering
Use fiscal_year for labeling; fy_label is NOT a calendar year


gross_exposure_up_to
Maximum MIGA liability under issued contracts (US$ millions)
NOT a loan; NOT capital received by Costa Rica


description
MIGA guarantee description
From MIGA project brief


investor_country
Country of origin of investor



in_scope
fy_label >= 1980 & fy_label <= 2025
Based on fiscal year label; see FY convention note






Project 3639 (Grupo del Istmo de Papagayo) appeared in FY2001, FY2002, and FY2003 with escalating cumulative exposures ($16.4M, $38.3M, $81M). The FY2001 and FY2002 rows were removed; the FY2003 row ($81M) represents the most complete disclosure. Summing all three rows would overcount by approximately $136M.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
US GDP deflator (data/processed/us_gdp_deflator.csv)
Unit: One row per year (1960–2025).








Variable
Definition
Notes




year
Calendar year
Integer


defl
US GDP deflator index
Indicator NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS from World Bank API. Base year 2020 = 100 (per API response). Annual.



Formula for converting nominal to real:
real_2025 = nominal * (defl[year==2025] / defl[year==approval_year])
2025 deflator value: 122.36 (preliminary; may be revised).
